headline: Trump's ads cost taxpayers $12 million. The DNC sues.
summary: Since September, TV ads have promoted Trump and his message, the fifth tagged "paid for by the U.S. Government." AdImpact puts the cost so far above $12 million, from $20 million in Homeland Security money. On Wednesday the Democratic National Committee sued, calling the ads illegal propaganda. Trump says his super PAC pays from now on.

cover_question.q: Whose money paid for the ads?

cover_answer: Everyone's taxes. Trump says his own group pays next time.
table_question: Can you spend the team's money on a poster about yourself?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The president put ads on TV that say he is doing a great job. The money came from taxes, the money everyone chips in, like the jar on the counter the whole family puts coins in. Some people say he can't use that jar for ads about himself, so they asked a judge. Nothing changes for you.
5-7.why: The jar is the whole story at seven. Whose coins, and what for.
5-7.why_long: A seven-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script turns $20 million of federal money into the family coin jar on the counter: everyone chips in, and the rule is about what it is for. That is the one vivid feature they will keep. Expect "is he in trouble?" Not yet. A judge has to look first.

8-12.script: TV ads have praised Trump since September, tagged "paid for by the U.S. Government." They have cost over $12 million. A law says tax money can't buy "publicity or propaganda." The Democrats sued Wednesday, like a player asking the referee to open the rulebook.
8-12.why: A rule and a bill, then a referee.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out whether adults apply the rules, and the script hands them the chain: a rule from Congress, $20 million of public money, ads with the government's name on them, a lawsuit. The referee is the mechanism, since nobody in the game gets to call it. Expect "will he have to pay it back?" He says "we'll decide."

13-17.script: Where is the line between a public service announcement and a campaign ad? The White House says these are the first, like past presidents' ads. The DNC says they praise one man a month before the midterms, and sued. Second: Trump says his super PAC pays next time. Does that fix the $12 million?
13-17.why: Two names for one ad. Let them draw the line.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can reason about a line that is not in front of them, so the script hands them two true descriptions of one ad: a government announcement, as past presidents ran, and a campaign spot with one man's face on it a month before an election. Expect "did he break the law?" Nobody knows yet. The lawsuit was filed Wednesday.

5-7.q: Whose money paid for the ads?
5-7.a: Tax money, the jar everyone chips into. Some people say that's not allowed, so a judge will look.

8-12.a: Paid messages to make you like a leader. Tax money can't buy them.

8-12.q: How much did the ads cost?
8-12.a: Over $12 million so far, from $20 million at Homeland Security.

13-17.q: Haven't other presidents run government ads?
13-17.a: Yes. The White House says so. Past ads helped people use a program.
His super PAC pays next time, he says. Money spent: "we'll decide."
